inlines.text: 引言

blocks.text: 今年以来，AI 系统的能力不断增强，它们自身为 AI 研发做出贡献的潜力也随之提升。今天，我们基于对编程智能体如何加速并改变 AI 开发周期的内部测量，更新 OpenAI 在研究加速方面的现状。

blocks.text: 我们的主要发现：

inlines.text: 我们的主要发现：
智能体现在能独立完成近一半耗时两到四小时的研究任务，但人类在 AI 研发中依然处于核心位置。
从 3 月到 10 月，对于估计需要人类工作两到四小时的任务，估计成功率从 23% 升至 46%；对于估计需要四到八小时的任务，成功率从 13% 升至 35%。但工作类型很关键。例如，按任务类型细分，自主智能体的成功率在监控训练运行上为 79%，在启动训练运行上为 35%，在为推理和服务栈编写代码上为 25%。总体来看，提升幅度参差不齐，人类仍是 AI 研究闭环中的核心一环。
智能体的使用量激增，重度用户正进一步拉开差距。
按 API 标价计算，10 月研究人员的每日使用量中位数达到 2400 美元，较 9 月增长 62%；第 90 百分位达到 23000 美元，较 9 月增长 105%。一项调查从另一个角度说明了研究人员对这些工具的重视程度。当被问及愿意拿什么来换取继续使用前沿编程智能体三个月时，答案的中位数是团队算力的 30%，而在另一个单独问题中则是团队人力的 40%。
研究人员正把越来越多的人力投入到安全与对齐领域
，在 OpenAI 所有主要研究领域中，该领域有记录的研究投入绝对增幅最大。从 1 月到 9 月，安全与对齐领域有记录的工作周数增长了 77%，这既源于新招聘，也源于现有研究人员转向这些工作方向。在我们于 2026 年 7 月回应
Hugging Face 事件⁠
之后，增长明显加快。

blocks.text: 本报告建立在我们 9 月关于 OpenAI 研究加速⁠的博客文章之上，新增了定量与定性指标，分别衡量 (1) AI 在各研究领域带来的提升，以及 (2) 人类如何继续参与研究过程。总体而言，我们认为本次更新提供了更全面但仍不完整的图景，展示 OpenAI 的研究正在如何变化。

inlines.text: 内部智能体使用情况

blocks.text: 自我们的首份报告⁠发布以来，研究组织内部的智能体 AI 使用量持续呈指数级增长。按 API 标价计算，中位数研究者目前每天在智能体 AI 工具上花费约 2,400 美元，第 90 百分位研究者每天约 23,000 美元，较 9 月的 1,500 美元和 11,000 美元分别增长 62% 和 105%。2 这一智能体使用量增长的趋势涵盖了多种变化，包括活动量增加、转向更昂贵的模型，以及模型行为和智能体框架的调整。

blocks.text: 我们在九月的分析⁠中曾指出，智能体越来越有可能在无需人工干预的情况下成功完成任务，其中也包括估计需要数小时人工工作量的任务。采用更新后的方法（见下文方法部分），我们发现这一趋势总体仍在延续。重要的是，随着智能体能力增强，研究人员在每个时长区间内委托的任务类型也可能发生了变化。因此，这些区间内零干预成功率的变动，可能既反映了能力提升，也反映了研究人员在何时、如何使用智能体方面的选择变化。

inlines.text: 最后，为了获得工作流程变化的定性证据，我们还访谈了预训练、后训练和安全领域的十名研究人员，了解他们如何使用智能体。这些访谈中浮现出五个主要主题，总结如下：
研究人员用智能体实现代码、调试并监督实验：
“我曾经移植过一个开源评测，当时要想围绕‘这个评测到底好不好’做研究和消融实验，工作量要大得多。可能得花一周半到两周，才能真正回答‘我们能不能用这个评测？’而现在，视评测而定，从零到跑起来只要一天，也许几天。”
——研究员 7，安全方向，从事评测工作
智能体在研究想法、代码质量、数据质量和写作上的品味都不行：
“模型通常没法一次性提出自己解决不了的、表述清晰的问题。而且如果你让模型生成一个数据点一百次，它每次生成的数据点都差不多。”
——研究员 2，安全方向，从事强化学习环境工作
工作流需要人密切参与，才能避免低质量产出和无效循环：
智能体难以高效地启动实验，会在不必要的步骤上钻牛角尖，提交“AI 垃圾”PR，产出无法使用的数据工件，还会做出错误的分析假设。
“我试过说‘把这个任务做成那个任务那样’，结果被坑了太多次——做出来不太对，我还得改。现在我会说‘先做一个，我来审阅修改，然后再去做剩下的。’”
——研究员 1，后训练方向，从事评测工作
研究人员预计当前瓶颈领域会有显著改善：
“我确实觉得我在想法上更有品味。但我没信心这能持续多久。”
——研究员 8，预训练方向，从事架构和数据工作
研究人员认为大规模扫描和生成内容带来了大幅提升：
研究人员用模型扫描数千个样本，以诊断实验中的问题、标记令人担忧的模型行为实例，并构建和质检新数据集。
“我最近做的一件事是把我们所有数据都过了一遍……我让它跑了几轮，并校准了它给我的结果。……它给了我一张整理得非常好的大表格。……没有 AI 的话，这会非常痛苦。”
——研究员 3，后训练方向，从事数据质量工作

inlines.text: Introduction

blocks.text: Over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves. Today, we’re providing an update on the state of research acceleration at OpenAI, based on internal measurements of how coding agents have accelerated and changed the AI development cycle.

inlines.text: Over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves. Today, we’re providing an update on the state of research acceleration at OpenAI, based on internal measurements of how coding agents have accelerated and changed the AI development cycle.

blocks.text: Our biggest takeaways:

inlines.text: Our biggest takeaways:
Agents now complete nearly half of two-to-four-hour research tasks on their own. But humans are still central to AI development.

From March to October, estimated success rose from 23% to 46% for tasks estimated to require two to four hours of human work, and rose from 13% to 35% for tasks estimated to require four to eight hours. But the kind of work matters. For example, in a task-level breakdown, the autonomous agent success rate was 79% for monitoring training runs, 35% for launching training runs, and 25% for writing code for inference and serving stacks. Overall, uplift is jagged, and humans remain a core part of the AI research loop.
Agent use is surging, and the heaviest users are pulling further ahead.

At API list prices, the median researcher’s daily usage reached $2,400 in October, up 62% from September. At the 90th percentile it reached $23,000, up 105% from September. A survey gives us another indication of how much researchers value these tools. Asked what they would trade to keep frontier coding agents for three months, the median answers were 30% of team compute or, in a separate question, 40% of team headcount.
Researchers are devoting increasing human effort to Safety and Alignment

, which saw the largest absolute increase in documented research efforts across all of OpenAI’s major research areas. Safety and Alignment’s documented workweeks increased by 77% from January to September due to both new hires and existing researchers shifting towards these workstreams. Growth picked up significantly following our response to the
Hugging Face incident⁠
in July 2026.

blocks.text: As capabilities improve and dramatic AI-driven research acceleration becomes increasingly possible, we will need to solve novel technical and governance issues to maintain human oversight and safely scale AI systems⁠. Transparency about indicators of RSI is therefore essential to inform a public discussion of the capabilities, risks, and required safeguards for increasingly powerful AI; however, our reporting should not be read as an intention to pursue full RSI. inlines.text: Inputs

blocks.text: AI research uses several inputs, including data, AI tools (e.g., coding agents), human labor, and compute. In this report, we focus on AI tools as an input to research. Specifically, we document how the intensity of coding-agent use varies across teams and changes over time. blocks.text: To better understand how agent use might affect research productivity, we next examine how the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI is changing. The productivity gains from new technologies depend in part on how work is reorganized around them. As agents improve, researchers may change which tasks they delegate to AI, how they oversee and coordinate agents’ work, and which projects they pursue. Below, we report both quantitative and qualitative measures of how AI is changing the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI. Together, these different types of data contribute to a (partial) view of how researchers are reorganizing their work around agents and how researchers remain in the loop today.

blocks.text: Alongside these trends by estimated duration, we also examine how success varies across the different types of tasks researchers might choose to delegate. We report estimated success rates by category and task, using the O*NET AI R&D taxonomy⁠(opens in a new window) developed by Epoch AI. Unsurprisingly, our results suggest that models are not equally good across all task categories: for instance, from August 1, 2026 through October 18, 2026, estimated success rates without human intervention was higher for Communicate (69%) and Analyze (58%) than for Build (43%). Similarly at the task level, estimated success rates were higher for tasks such as monitoring runs for issues (79%) and answering technical questions (72%), whereas they were lower for writing code for inference and serving stacks (25%) and building evaluation, reinforcement-learning, and agent environments (29%). So long as model performance on AI R&D-related tasks is heterogeneous, lower-performing categories and tasks could become bottlenecks to high overall uplift.

inlines.text: Lastly, to capture qualitative evidence on workflow changes, we also interviewed ten researchers from pretraining, posttraining, and safety on how they used agents. Across these interviews, five main themes emerged, which we summarize below:
Researchers use agents to implement code and debug and oversee experiments:

“I once ported an open-source eval where it was much more involved to get studies and ablations on 'is this a good eval'. It might have been a week and a half or two to really get to the point of “Can we use this or not?” Whereas now, depending on the eval, zero to running it is a day, maybe a few days.”
—Researcher 7, safety, working on evaluations
Agents have poor taste in research ideas, code quality, data quality, and writing:

“The model generally can’t one-shot come up with well-posed problems that it cannot solve itself. And if you ask the model to generate a data point a hundred times, it’ll generate similar data points each time.”
—Researcher 2, safety, working on reinforcement learning environments
Workflows require close human involvement to avoid low-quality outputs and wasted cycles:
agents struggled to launch experiments efficiently, rabbit-holed on unnecessary steps, wrote “AI slop” PRs, produced unusable data artifacts, and made invalid analysis assumptions.

“I've tried saying, ‘Just make this task like this other task,’ and been burned too many times when it's not quite right and I need to make edits. Now I say, ‘Go make one. I'll review it and make edits. Then go do the rest.’”
—Researcher 1, posttraining, working on evaluations
Researchers expected significant improvements in current bottleneck areas:
“I do think I have more taste in terms of the ideas. But I have no confidence that will continue to be true for any significant period of time.”
—Researcher 8, pretraining, working on architecture and data
Researchers see large uplift from scanning and generating content at scale:
researchers used models to scan thousands of samples to diagnose issues in experiments, flag concerning instances of model behavior, and build and QC new datasets.

“One thing I did recently was look through all of our data… I had it do a couple of rounds and calibrated what it was giving me. … It gave me a really nice, giant sheet with everything organized. … Without AI, this would have been super painful.”
—Researcher 3, posttraining, working on data quality

blocks.text: Beyond changes in research inputs and workflows, we also want to understand whether AI use is accelerating research progress. To inform this question, we present three measures. Two of them—lines of code and the number of research experiments—were included in our September analysis⁠. These measures are straightforward to track, but increases in these measures of research activity do not necessarily imply faster research progress. We therefore also introduce OpenAI ECI, an OpenAI-specific internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index, which is one methodology to track changes in model capabilities as a more direct measure of research outcomes.

blocks.text: Conclusion

inlines.text: Conclusion

blocks.text: Overall, our findings extend the picture from our September report⁠: researchers are using agents more intensively, delegating more work, and adapting their workflows around models’ capabilities and limitations. However, this uplift isn’t uniform across all research workflows, and agents today still have significant flaws.

blocks.text: We note that the historical trends and metrics we report (which involve significant human-AI collaboration) may not be predictive of future AI-driven progress. For instance, we recently saw sudden and rapid breakthroughs in mathematics⁠ produced by frontier models. As our models become increasingly autonomous and capable for research, we are monitoring for similarly rapid breakthroughs in deep learning.
